findings.antecedent: Binaural listening
findings.quote: The binaural thresholds of hearing shown in Figure 11-1 and Table 11-1 are approximately 2 dB lower than the corresponding monaural thresholds if both ears have similar sensitivity

findings.antecedent: Increasing frequency (for low frequency stimuli)
findings.quote: The audibility of low frequency stimuli improves with increasing frequency at an average rate of about 12 dB/octave

findings.antecedent: Age (for high frequency stimuli)
findings.quote: The audibility of stimuli with frequencies in the upper end of the frequency range varies quite a bit with individuals and decreases substantially with age

findings.antecedent: Acoustic resonances of the ear canal and concha
findings.quote: The high sensitivity of the auditory system in this frequency range results from acoustic resonances of the ear canal and concha

findings.antecedent: Occluding the ear canal by an earphone
findings.quote: occluding the ear canal by an earphone was reported to cause an amplification of low frequency physiologic noise (e.g., blood flow noise) by the closed cavity of the ear canal and elevation of MAP threshold at low frequencies

findings.antecedent: Bone conduction stimulation by impinging sound waves
findings.consequent: Intensity required for same sensation as air conduction
findings.quote: In the case of bone conduction stimulation by impinging sound waves, such sound waves need to be 40 to 50 dB more intense than those causing the same sensation though the air conduction pathways.

findings.antecedent: Background noise level (in 30 to 70 dB SPL range)
findings.quote: According to Gardner (1964), the threshold of discomfort is almost independent of background noise level (in 30 to 70 dB SPL range) and exceeds 80 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: Increasing sound intensity (for 1-kHz tone at moderate/high levels)
findings.quote: for moderate and high intensity levels the loudness of a 1-kHz tone doubles when its sound pressure level increases by about 10 dB (Stevens, 1955).

findings.antecedent: Neurophysiologic hearing loss
findings.quote: individuals with neurophysiologic hearing loss have elevated thresholds of hearing but still have about the same or even lower threshold of pain. These shifts in thresholds result in a narrower dynamic range of hearing and in a loudness function that has to have a steeper slope than that of normally hearing individuals.

findings.antecedent: Sound duration (for sounds shorter than critical duration)
findings.quote: For sounds shorter than critical duration, the loudness of sound increases with sound duration

findings.antecedent: Higher repetition rate and shorter duration (of clicks/noise bursts)
findings.quote: bursts of higher repetition rate and shorter duration have been reported to sound louder than the same bursts of longer duration and slower repetition rate

findings.antecedent: Auditory stimulus acting for a prolonged period of time (after temporal integration)
findings.quote: if the auditory stimulus acts for a prolonged period of time, the sensation of loudness slightly decreases.

findings.antecedent: Masker intensity
findings.consequent: Masked threshold (for pure tone masked by wideband noise)
findings.quote: When the masker contains sufficient energy in the frequency region of the target sound, the masked threshold increases about 10 dB for every 10 dB increase in masker.

findings.antecedent: Masker and target sound frequency proximity
findings.quote: The closer the masker and target sound are on the frequency scale, the greater the masking.

findings.antecedent: Bandwidth of narrowband masker (up to critical band limit)
findings.quote: As the bandwidth of the narrowband masker increases, its masking effectiveness increases until its bandwidth exceeds the limits of the critical band

findings.antecedent: Simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands
findings.quote: simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands aids signal detection.

findings.antecedent: Masker intensity
findings.quote: Masking decreases as the intensity of the masker decreases

findings.antecedent: Time difference between masker offset and target onset
findings.quote: Masking decreases as... the time difference between the two offsets increases.

findings.antecedent: Additional tone added to masker outside critical band of target tone
findings.quote: the level of forward masking exerted by one tone on the subsequent tone can be decreased if additional tone is added to the masker in the region outside of the critical band of the target tone

findings.antecedent: Similarity between masker and target sound
findings.quote: Two main causes of informational masking are similarity between the masker and the target sound and the variability (uncertainty) of the masker

findings.antecedent: Masker uncertainty (spectro-temporal or spatial)
findings.quote: Two main causes of informational masking are similarity between the masker and the target sound and the variability (uncertainty) of the masker

findings.antecedent: Number of voices in multitalker noise (MTN) (up to ~10 voices)
findings.quote: masking effectiveness of an MTN increases with the number of voices, reaches its plateau for about 10 voices and then declines.

findings.antecedent: Age (older individuals, age 60+)
findings.consequent: Informational masking effectiveness (for speech recognition in IM background)
findings.quote: IM effectiveness increases with age even in people with otologically normal hearing. Rajan and Cainer (2008) reported that with aging, independent of any hearing loss, older individuals (age 60 or greater) performed as well as younger individuals in speech recognition in an energetic masking background but performed much poorer in the presence of informational maskers.

findings.antecedent: Frequency separation between individual tones (smaller than critical band, max ~1/4 critical band)
findings.quote: Dissonance occurs if the frequency separation between the individual tones of the sound is smaller than a critical band with its maximum for tones separation equal about ¼ of the critical band

findings.antecedent: Increased sound intensity (for higher frequencies)
findings.quote: for tones of higher frequencies, increased sound intensity produces an increase in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Increased sound intensity (for lower frequencies)
findings.quote: Conversely, for tones of lower frequencies, increased sound intensity produces a decrease in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Dynamic changes in sound intensity and frequency (Doppler shifted tones)
findings.quote: Neuhoff's data suggest that pitch and loudness are perceived integrally (i.e., changes in one dimension can be perceived as changes in the other)

findings.antecedent: Frequency components separated by more than one critical band
findings.quote: people are sensitive to neither absolute nor relative phase difference between various components of the periodic stimulus if the components are separated in their frequencies by more than one critical band.

findings.antecedent: Two frequency components falling into the same critical band (small frequency difference)
findings.quote: if two frequency components, e.g., harmonics, fall into the same critical band and their difference in frequency is rather small, the changes in their phase relationship are audible and affect both pitch value and pitch clarity

findings.antecedent: Sound source approaches listener
findings.consequent: Frequency of sound reaching listener's ears
findings.quote: As the sound source approaches the listener, the compressions and rarefaction of the produced sound wave become compressed, making the frequency of the sound reaching the listener's ears higher than the frequency of the actually emitted sound.

findings.antecedent: Sound source moves away from listener
findings.consequent: Frequency of sound reaching listener's ears
findings.quote: As the sound source passes the listener and moves away, the distances between the compressions and rarefactions of the sound wave became stretched, making the frequency of the sound reaching the listener's ears lower that the frequency of the emitted sound.

findings.antecedent: Listener moves his or her head while sound is present
findings.consequent: Auditory system disambiguating information for sound localization
findings.quote: Even if a sound is unfamiliar, the auditory system can gain disambiguating information if the listener moves his or her head while the sound is present

findings.antecedent: Small head movements
findings.consequent: Clarification of front/rear hemisphere sound location
findings.quote: Small movements of the head from the left to the right will quickly clarify whether the sound is in the front or rear hemisphere.

findings.antecedent: Vertical head movements
findings.quote: Vertical movements give salient elevation information

findings.antecedent: Second sound delayed up to about 30 to 40 ms, intensity not exceeding first sound by more than 10 dB
findings.quote: The precedence effect is the phenomenon that the perception of the second of two successively received similar sounds is suppressed if the second sound is delayed up to about 30 to 40 ms, and its intensity does not exceed the intensity of the first sound by more than 10 dB.

findings.antecedent: Time delay of lagging sound (between 1 and 5 ms)
findings.consequent: Sound appears to be coming from only the lead loudspeaker
findings.quote: When the time delay of the lagging sound is between 1 and 5 ms, the sound appears to be coming from only the lead loudspeaker, but its timbre and depth perception change.

findings.antecedent: Time delay of lagging sound (more than 5 ms but less than 30 ms)
findings.consequent: Only the first sound is heard
findings.quote: if the time delay of the second sound is more than 5 ms but less than 30 ms, depending on the specific environment, only the first sound is heard, and the second sound has no effect.

findings.antecedent: Lagging sound (more than 10 to 15 dB more intense than leading sound)
findings.consequent: Only the second sound and its direction are heard
findings.quote: if the lagging sound is more than 10 to 15 dB more intense than the leading sound, only the second sound and its direction are heard

findings.antecedent: Lagging sound delayed (longer than about 30 ms) and sounds are very similar
findings.consequent: Second sound heard as an echo of the first sound
findings.quote: If the time delay is longer than about 30 ms and the sounds are very similar, the second sound is heard as an echo of the first sound.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with original signal and surrounding space
findings.consequent: Sound localization ability (especially vertical plane and front-back axis)
findings.quote: sound localization ability, especially in the vertical plane and along the front-back axis, improves with experience and familiarization with both the stimuli and environment

findings.antecedent: Lack of familiarity with specific auditory stimuli
findings.consequent: Front-back confusions and poor localization in vertical plane
findings.quote: The lack of familiarity with specific auditory stimuli is reported frequently in the literature as the secondary reason for front-back confusions and poor localization in vertical plane.

findings.antecedent: Distance to sound source (in open space)
findings.quote: According to the inverse square law of sound propagation in open space, sound intensity decreases by 6 dB per doubling of the distance from the sound source.

findings.antecedent: Distance to sound source
findings.quote: Consequently, distant sounds will have relatively more low frequency energy than the same sounds radiated from proximal (nearby) sound sources and result in different sound timbre.

findings.antecedent: Distance to sound source (in closed spaces)
findings.quote: If the sound source is located close to the listener, the direct-to-reverberant sound ratio is high... If the distance is large, the sound becomes less clear

findings.antecedent: Listener moves head
findings.consequent: Change in azimuth toward sound source
findings.quote: when the listener moves (translates) the head, the change in the azimuth toward the sound source is distance dependent.

findings.antecedent: Larger distance to sound source
findings.consequent: Relative error in auditory distance estimation
findings.quote: people underestimate the distance to the sound source in an exponential manner – the larger the distance to the sound source the larger relative error

findings.antecedent: Perceived auditory distance to another talker in an audio channel (different from 1 to 1.5 m)
findings.quote: If the perceived auditory distance to another talker in an audio channel is quite different from 1 to 1.5 m, such voice communication will distract the operator, increase the workload, and increase the overall level of anxiety.

findings.antecedent: Anomalies in the outer ear
findings.quote: anomalies in the outer can impede the listener's ability to localize.

findings.antecedent: Lower speech test complexity, quieter background noise
findings.quote: As the speech test complexity gets lower and the background noise gets quieter, the SRT decreases.

findings.antecedent: More contextual information and higher degree of redundancy (in speech material)
findings.quote: Speech intelligibility performance generally improves as the material becomes more complex and contains more contextual information and higher degree of redundancy

findings.antecedent: Trained talker
findings.quote: A trained talker such as radio announcer who speaks clearly will be more intelligible than a talker using normal conversational speech.

findings.antecedent: Female voice
findings.quote: a female voice is generally more intelligible than a male voice

findings.antecedent: Trained listeners
findings.quote: Trained listeners who are familiar with the test and the speech material to be tested will perform best and have the most reliable scores

findings.antecedent: Impaired hearing
findings.quote: Listeners who have impaired hearing will perform differently than normal hearing counterparts

findings.antecedent: Noise levels (up to 40 dB SPL)
findings.quote: noise levels up to 40 dB SPL have a negligible effect on the MCL for speech.

findings.antecedent: Noise levels (above 40 dB SPL)
findings.quote: MCL increases about 7 dB per 10 dB of increase in noise levels, up to about 100 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: High SNR
findings.quote: Good understanding of speech requires high SNRs in the order of 15 to 30 dB.

findings.antecedent: Random, unpredictable noise or noise with speech-like characteristics
findings.quote: random, unpredictable noise, or noise where the temporal and spectral characteristics are similar to that of speech, can add informational masking to the energetic masking.

findings.antecedent: Spatial separation of speech information from noise
findings.quote: the listener can use spatial localization cues (described later in this chapter) to separate the speech information from the noise and can attend to the spatial location of the speech

findings.antecedent: Low frequency limit of channel transmitting speech signal
findings.quote: changes of low frequency limit of the channel transmitting speech signal have small if any effect on speech intelligibility but can greatly affect speech quality.

findings.antecedent: Longer lasting events (exceeding several seconds)
findings.quote: pleasant events appear to last shorter (time contraction) and unpleasant events longer (time dilation) than their actual physical durations.

findings.antecedent: Very short acoustic events
findings.quote: In the case of very short acoustic events, humans have a general tendency to overestimate sound duration

findings.antecedent: Short pauses
findings.quote: short pauses seem to last as much as 2 to 4 times longer than short sound bursts of the same duration

findings.antecedent: Higher frequency of sound
findings.consequent: Perceptual difference in perceived duration of pauses vs sound bursts
findings.quote: The higher the frequency of the sound, the greater this perceptual difference.

findings.antecedent: Longer temporal gaps between signals
findings.quote: regardless of whether the judgment is quantitative or qualitative, longer temporal gaps between signals lead to larger variability in listener judgments

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with a specific sound source's voice
findings.quote: if a listener is familiar with somebody's voice, this familiarity may help the listener to differentiate whether the talker is located in front or behind the listener.

findings.antecedent: Narrowband stimuli presented within the medial sagittal plane
findings.consequent: Tendency to associate with front, rear, or overhead locations
findings.quote: Blauert (2001) observed that narrowband stimuli presented within the medial sagittal plane have the tendency to be associated with the front, rear, or overhead, regardless of the actual position of the sound source.
